opus-5.5.text:
Well, the core issue is that any benchmark you put out into the world starts to degrade the moment people can see it. If all the tasks are public, you get leakage. Not necessarily through anyone cheating, but through the sheer process of the community iterating on the same data. People tune their approaches, the tasks end up in training corpora, and over time your scores stop measuring what you designed them to measure. You end up measuring memorization, or at least familiarity, rather than the ability to adapt to novelty, which is the whole point of ARC.

So the three-set structure is about separating different kinds of trust.

First, you have a **public evaluation set**. It lets researchers develop, debug, and get a rough sense of where they stand. It's fully transparent. But you should assume it's compromised in the long run, because everyone can see it.

Second, there's a **semi-private set**. We use it for verifying results from systems we can't run in a sealed environment, like frontier models behind an API. We have to send those tasks to a third party's servers, so we can't guarantee they never leak. It's more trustworthy than the public set, but not fully trustworthy.

Third, there's a **fully private set** that never leaves our controlled environment. That's what we use for the competition, where solutions run offline with no internet access. It's the gold standard: the tasks have never been seen by anyone outside the evaluation process.

And critically, we tried to calibrate the three sets to be of similar difficulty. That way, if a system does much better on the public set than on the semi-private or private sets, it tells you something. It's a signal of overfitting or contamination rather than genuine generalization. The gap between the sets becomes informative in itself.

So it's really about making sure the benchmark stays meaningful over time. If you want to measure fluid intelligence, the ability to handle problems you've never seen before, then you have to guarantee that the problems really are unseen. The three-set protocol is how we try to keep that guarantee honest.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the whole point of ARC is to measure something that benchmarks usually fail to measure, which is the ability to adapt to novelty. And the moment you have a public benchmark that people are optimizing against, you have a problem, because the benchmark stops measuring generalization and starts measuring how well you've fit the benchmark. So with ARC-2 we were very deliberate about how we split the data.

You have the public training set, which is really there to teach you the priors, the core knowledge the tasks assume. Objectness, counting, basic geometry, that kind of thing. It's not meant to be representative of the test distribution in any precise sense. It's a curriculum.

Then you have the public evaluation set, which is harder, and which is there so people can iterate, so they can actually develop their approach and get a signal. But of course, anything public is going to leak. It ends up in training corpora, people overfit to it, consciously or not. So you can't trust numbers on it as a measure of true generalization.

And then you have the private evaluation set, which nobody has seen, which is only run on Kaggle under compute constraints, and that is the only number we really stand behind. It's the control, essentially. The difference between public eval and private eval scores is actually very informative. If a system does well on the public set and collapses on the private set, that tells you it was memorizing, or that it was tuned to specifics of the tasks it had access to, and not acquiring a general skill.

We also added a semi-private set this time, which we use to evaluate the commercial frontier models through their APIs, because we can't run those offline. It's not perfectly secure, since the data does go over the wire, but it's not something that's sitting in a GitHub repo either. So it gives us a reasonable estimate for closed models.

And the other important thing with ARC-2 is calibration. Every task in all three sets was tested on humans. We only kept tasks that at least two people could solve within a couple of attempts, so we know they're doable, and we know the difficulty is roughly matched across the sets. That matters, because if your private set is accidentally much harder than your public set, you can't interpret the gap. You want the gap to reflect generalization and nothing else.

So it's really about one thing: making sure that when we report a number, it means what we claim it means. Intelligence is efficiency of skill acquisition on things you haven't seen before. If the test has been seen, you're not measuring intelligence anymore, you're measuring memory.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to separate development from evaluation, and then to separate evaluation from final verification. Once you use a benchmark to guide your research—even if you never train on its examples—you start adapting to it. You try different approaches, keep the ones that improve the score, and the benchmark becomes part of your optimization process.

So you want a public evaluation set that people can experiment with, a private set that provides more controlled feedback, and a third, held-out set that you use for final verification. That last set should not be giving you a signal throughout development.

For ARC, this matters because what we're trying to measure is the ability to adapt to unfamiliar tasks. If your system has effectively been selected to fit the evaluation tasks, you're no longer measuring quite the same thing. The three-set protocol helps distinguish genuine generalization from adaptation to the benchmark.

sol-6.1.text:
The reason is that once you use an evaluation set to guide your research, it’s effectively becoming a training set. You try an approach, look at the score, change something, and try again. Even if you never directly train on those examples, you’re adapting to them.

So you want three sets with distinct roles: a public set for development, a private set for evaluating submissions, and a third, held-out set that isn’t part of that feedback loop. That last set lets you check whether progress on the benchmark actually transfers to fresh tasks, or whether you’ve been overfitting to the evaluation process.

For ARC, that distinction is central. We’re trying to measure the ability to adapt to novelty. If the tasks are no longer truly novel to the research process, the score becomes much harder to interpret.
